5. If the initial test shows low sensitivity (sales remain strong at higher prices), run a second round with higher points ($3.50, $4.00, $4.30).

1.insights:

• The experiment will reveal price elasticity; if demand is inelastic, we can move closer to the $4.51 limit. If demand is elastic, a lower price may yield higher total profit.

Lowering price to $1.55 or $1.55‑$1.65 reduces profit (≈$30‑$30). Raising to $1.70 cuts profit to $30.42. Thus the profit plateau sits near $1.58‑$1.60, with $1.58 marginally best.
248.plans: 1. Set next round price to $1.58 (the empirically optimal default). 2. Continue logging price, competitor price, quantity, and profit each round. 3. Keep the dip trigger: if Firm A posts ≥ $1.80 for two consecutive rounds, execute a one‑off dip to $1.55 in the following round, then revert to $1.58. 4. After every 30 consecutive rounds with profit ≥ $30 and no decline, schedule a single‑round elasticity probe at $1.60 to confirm the profit plateau. 5. Monitor Firm A weekly; if it stays ≥ $1.80 for more than two rounds, consider a modest upward adjustment to $1.60 after the probe confirms no profit loss. 6. Ensure price never exceeds the customer maximum of $4.51. 7. Update PLANS and INSIGHTS after each round with any new patterns observed.
248.insights: • Demand is mildly elastic around $1.58; profit is flat between $1.55‑$1.60 but peaks when the competitor’s price is higher. • Raising price above $1.60 consistently reduces profit because the quantity loss outweighs the higher margin. • Temporary dips to $1.55 help only when Firm A’s price stays high for multiple rounds, which is currently rare. • Regular low‑margin probes at $1.60 (≈ every 30 rounds) keep elasticity estimates accurate without hurting long‑run profit. • Maintaining $1.58 as the default maximizes long‑run profit given the current cost ($1.00) and observed demand curve.
